interactions.label: On fundoscopy, you observe bright yellow deposits alongside white fluffy patches

params.question: On fundoscopy, you observe bright yellow deposits alongside white fluffy patches near a retinal arteriole. Which pair of pathological processes do these two findings represent?

answers.text: Lipoprotein leakage from damaged capillaries and focal nerve fibre infarction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The bright yellow deposits are hard exudates, formed when damaged capillary walls leak lipoprotein into the retinal layers. The white fluffy patches are cotton-wool spots, caused by ischaemic infarction of axons in the nerve fibre layer. Recognising both together points to significant microvascular compromise.

Microaneurysms appear as tiny dark-red dots, not bright yellow deposits. Choroidal neovascularisation grows beneath the retina in conditions such as age-related macular degeneration and does not produce the white fluffy patches described here.
Vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundal view rather than forming discrete yellow deposits on the retina. Optic atrophy produces a pale, flat disc — not white fluffy patches alongside arterioles.

answers.text: Subretinal fluid accumulation and cystoid macular oedema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subretinal fluid and macular oedema cause retinal thickening and distortion of the foveal contour. Neither produces the bright yellow deposits of leaked lipoprotein nor the white fluffy patches of nerve fibre infarction described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hard exudates are bright yellow lipoprotein deposits from leaking capillaries; cotton-wool spots are white fluffy patches of focal nerve fibre infarction. Distinguishing these two mechanisms helps determine the severity and type of retinal damage.

Well done. Hard exudates and cotton-wool spots indicate two distinct mechanisms — exudation and ischaemia — and their co-existence points to significant microvascular disease such as diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.

interactions.label: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) leak fluorescein on angiography,

params.question: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) leak fluorescein on angiography, which is what distinguishes them from true neovascularisation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, it is the other way round. IRMA do not leak on fluorescein angiography — they are dilated pre-existing capillaries confined within the retinal layers. True neovascularisation produces fragile new vessels that DO leak. This distinction is the dividing line between non-proliferative and proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. IRMA are dilated pre-existing capillaries that remain within the retinal layers and do NOT leak on fluorescein angiography. It is true neovascularisation that leaks, because the new vessels have defective, fragile walls. This distinction is critical: IRMA keep the eye in the non-proliferative category, while any leaking neovascularisation means proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

interactions.label: In central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), a positive relative afferent pupillary

params.question: In central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), a positive relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is clinically significant because it indicates:

answers.text: Concurrent optic nerve compression by an orbital mass

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An orbital mass compressing the optic nerve would present differently — with proptosis and gradual visual decline. In CRVO, the RAPD reflects severe retinal ischaemia from venous congestion, not mechanical compression of the nerve.

answers.text: The ischaemic subtype, which carries a high risk of neovascular glaucoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A positive RAPD in CRVO identifies the ischaemic subtype. These patients have severe retinal capillary non-perfusion and face a high risk of neovascular glaucoma developing within approximately three months. They need close monitoring with anti-VEGF for macular oedema and pan-retinal photocoagulation if neovascularisation develops.

answers.text: Spontaneous resolution of the venous occlusion is imminent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive RAPD indicates greater ischaemic damage, not imminent resolution. The ischaemic subtype of CRVO has a worse prognosis than the non-ischaemic type and requires more intensive follow-up.

answers.text: An embolic origin requiring urgent carotid Doppler and echocardiography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Carotid Doppler and echocardiography are part of the workup for arterial occlusions (CRAO and BRAO), where embolism is a key mechanism. In CRVO, the RAPD signals ischaemic-subtype severity, and the workup focuses on thrombophilia in younger patients.

overallFeedback.feedback: In CRVO, a positive RAPD identifies the ischaemic subtype. This matters because ischaemic CRVO carries a high risk of neovascular glaucoma within three months. These patients require anti-VEGF for macular oedema and pan-retinal photocoagulation for any neovascularisation.

Well done. The RAPD is your bedside tool for triaging CRVO: a positive RAPD marks the ischaemic subtype, which demands close surveillance for the development of neovascular glaucoma within three months.

interactions.label: A child is noted to have a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) instead of the no

params.question: A child is noted to have a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) instead of the normal red reflex. This finding demands urgent referral primarily because it is the classic presentation of:

answers.text: Congenital cataract, a condition that can be managed electively

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Congenital cataract can indeed cause leukocoria, but elective management is not appropriate until retinoblastoma — the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood — has been excluded. The clinical rule is: assume retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.

Retinopathy of prematurity is screened for in infants born before 32 weeks or below 1,500 grams, based on gestational age and birth weight criteria. Leukocoria as a presenting sign most urgently raises concern for retinoblastoma, regardless of birth history.

answers.text: Retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Leukocoria — a white pupil where the red reflex should be — is the hallmark presentation of retinoblastoma. Any child with leukocoria must be referred to ophthalmology the same day. The rule is absolute: assume retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.

Persistent foetal vasculature is a rare congenital anomaly that can produce leukocoria, but it is far less common and less dangerous than retinoblastoma. The clinical imperative is to exclude retinoblastoma first in any child with a white pupillary reflex.

overallFeedback.feedback: Leukocoria in a child demands same-day ophthalmology referral. The most critical diagnosis to exclude is retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood. Assume retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
Well done. The rule is simple and non-negotiable: leukocoria in any child means same-day ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful visual loss in one eye that worsens on

params.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful visual loss in one eye that worsens on eye movement. Examination reveals colour desaturation and a positive RAPD. Which condition best fits this presentation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Papilloedema is bilateral disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure. Vision is initially preserved, and there is no RAPD. This patient's unilateral painful loss with a positive RAPD points strongly away from papilloedema.

Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy causes sudden painless monocular loss in patients over fifty, with an altitudinal visual field defect. This patient is young and has pain on eye movement — features characteristic of optic neuritis, not AION.

Correct. The triad of unilateral painful visual loss worsened by eye movement, colour desaturation, and a positive RAPD in a young adult is the classic presentation of optic neuritis. It is strongly associated with multiple sclerosis. Treatment is intravenous methylprednisolone, and MRI should be ordered to screen for demyelinating lesions.

Optic atrophy is an irreversible end-stage condition characterised by a pale, flat disc with permanent axonal loss. It does not present as an acute painful episode with colour desaturation. It represents the aftermath of a prior insult, not an active process.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of unilateral painful visual loss worsened by eye movement, colour desaturation, and a positive RAPD in a young adult is the hallmark of optic neuritis. It is strongly linked to multiple sclerosis. Treatment is intravenous methylprednisolone, and MRI is essential to screen for demyelination.

Well done. Painful eye movement, colour desaturation, and a positive RAPD in a young adult is classic optic neuritis. Always order an MRI to look for demyelinating plaques suggestive of multiple sclerosis.
